headline: A bank is “money” plus “business establishment” — and that 行 is not the one that means “go”.

sources.quote: 銀 (gin, “medium of exchange; money”) + 行 (kō, “business establishment; firm”)

headline: “Economy” is two characters borrowed from a phrase about running a state and relieving the people's suffering.

sources.quote: From Middle Chinese 經濟 (keng tsejH), short for 經世濟民 (“to administer the state to relieve the suffering of the people”), through its use as a translation of English economics by Japanese scholars during the Meiji period.

headline: “Society” began as a gathering to honor the god of the earth, until a writer repurposed it in 1875.

sources.quote: From Middle Chinese 社會 (MC dzyaeX hwajH, “public gathering for offering to the god of earth”), as a compound composed of 社 (dzyae^X, “god of earth; ceremony for offering to the god of earth”) + 會 (“gathering”). The word was repurposed by Fukuchi Gen'ichirō in 1875 to translate the western concept of society.

headline: “Science” was coined in Japan from Chinese parts — and it collided with “chemistry”.

morphemes.meaning: field, imperial examination, compounding the radical 斗 (“measuring tool

sources.quote: /kʷaɡaku/ → /kaɡaku/
First attested in the mid-Meiji period as a translation of English science.
Coined in Japan of Middle Chinese-derived elements 科(か) (ka, “field, imperial examination, compounding the radical 斗 (“measuring tool”)”) + 学(がく) (-gaku, “school, study”).

headline: Nishi Amane coined “philosophy” in 1874 — after first trying a spelling that copies the Greek.

sources.quote: By surface analysis, 哲(てつ) (tetsu, “clear, wise, sage”) + 学(がく) (-gaku, “study”). Coined by Nishi Amane in his 1874 百一新論 as a translation of English philosophy or Dutch filosofie. Nishi's kanji spelling 希哲學 (hirosohi) is literally calqued from Ancient Greek φιλοσοφία (philosophía, “pursuit of wisdom”, literally “love of knowledge”), apparently from the Chinese morphemes 希 (xī, “to long for”) and 哲 (zhé, “wisdom”), before he later settled with 哲學 (modernly spelt 哲学).
Nishi also used the transcriptions ヒロソヒ, ヒロソヒー (hirosohī) and 斐鹵蘇比.

headline: Fireworks are “flower fire”, and the fire voices to び on the way in.

sources.quote: Compound of 花(はな) (hana, “flower”) + 火(ひ) (hi, “fire”). The hi changes to bi as an instance of rendaku (連濁).

headline: A lover is a “love person” — with the person voiced to びと.

sources.quote: From 恋(こい) (koi, “love”) + 人(ひと) (-hito, “person”). The hito changes to bito as an instance of rendaku (連濁).

headline: “Pure red” — a prefix that means “true”, glued to あか.

sources.quote: Compound of 真(ま)っ (ma'-, “true, pure”) + 赤(あか) (aka, “red”).
First cited to the mid-1400s.
The outright sense arose from the way that something purely red is obvious and clearly visible.

headline: The voicing landed one syllable late: not てづたう, but てつだう.

sources.quote: Compound of 手 (te, “hand”) + 伝う (tsutau, “to go along something (intransitive); to move something along, to transmit something (transitive)”).

The expected form of such a compound would be either てつたう (tetsutau), or てづたう (tezutau) with rendaku. The actual attested form of てつだう (tetsudau) suggests metathesis, with the voicing of rendaku shifting from the tsu to the following ta.
First attested in the late 1500s in 狂言 (kyōgen, “popular plays”).

headline: A room was once a “separate house” — へ plus や.

sources.quote: Originally a compound of へ (he, “separate”) + 屋(や) (ya, “roof; house”). The へ (he) is related to the first element in 隔(へだ)たる (hedataru, “to be apart, to be separated”). First attested in the late 900s.

headline: けさ is “this morning” — but the 今 in it is a stand-in for an older “this”.

sources.quote: From Old Japanese. Originally a compound of 此 (ke, “this”) + 朝 (asa, “morning”).

The initial /ke/ is an alternative form of the initial /ko/ (此, “this”) seen in words such as ここ (koko, “this place → here”) or これ (kore, “this [nominal] → this”), and the final /sa/ is a contraction from */ke.asa/ to /kesa/ with the medial -a- falling out, as Old Japanese did not permit vowel clusters.
It is the same element found in 今日 (kepu→kyō, “today”).
The use of the kanji 今 (“now”) instead of 此 (“this”) is an example of jukujikun (熟(じゅく)字(じ)訓(くん)).

headline: A stamp borrows its two characters from “ticket” and “commercial paper”.

sources.quote: From 切(きっ)符(ぷ) (kippu, “a ticket used for public transport”) + 手(て)形(がた) (tegata, “commercial paper”).

headline: Cherry blossoms may be named for what they do: bloom in bursts.

sources.quote: From Old Japanese, first attested in the Kojiki, the oldest extant historical record of ancient Japan, compiled in 712 CE.
Originally derived from 咲く (saku, “to bloom, burst open”) + 等 (-ra, nominalizing and pluralizing suffix).

headline: A can is probably a Dutch kan in a borrowed kanji — but Chinese is the other candidate.

sources.quote: Likely from Dutch kan (“cylindrical metallic container”), with additional influence from English can (“cylindrical metallic container”). The kanji is an example of ateji (当(あ)て字(じ)). Alternatively, from Middle Chinese 罐 (kuɑnH, “can; jar; tin”). The usage of 缶 is likely due to a 新字体 (shinjitai) simplification from earlier 旧字体 (kyūjitai) 罐, where the phonetic component 雚 was entirely eliminated.

headline: かぜ is just the word for “wind” — the 邪 is along for the spelling.

sources.quote: From 風(かぜ) (kaze, “wind”).
The kanji is jukujikun (熟(じゅく)字(じ)訓(くん)), from Chinese 風邪 /风邪 (fēngxié).
First attested in 984.

headline: Beer came in through Dutch, long before English.

sources.quote: Borrowing from Dutch bier.
First cited to a text from 1724 with the kanji spelling 麦酒 (literally “barley liquor”).

headline: A button is a Portuguese word, first written down in 1651.

sources.quote: Borrowed from Portuguese botão; compare English button.
First attested in 1651.

headline: ガラス is Dutch, and its English cousin has its own katakana word.

sources.quote: Borrowed from Dutch glas. Doublet of グラス.

headline: A glass tumbler with two possible parents, Dutch and Portuguese.

sources.quote: From Dutch kop and also from Portuguese copo. Doublet (via Late Latin cuppa) of カップ (kappu), from English cup.

headline: Curry reached Japan from English, but the word starts in Tamil.

sources.quote: From English curry, from Tamil கறி (kaṟi).

headline: Trousers are an “underskirt”: ズボン comes from French jupon.

sources.quote: Borrowed from French jupon (“petticoat, underskirt”), from French jupe (“skirt”), from old Italian jupa, from Arabic جُبَّة (jubba, “long garment”). Doublet of 襦袢.

Note that the meaning has changed from “underskirt” to “trousers/pants”, and the second consonant has changed from /p/ to /b/, possibly influenced by native Japanese onomatopoeia ずぼん (zubon), describing the action of something sliding into place, as when one puts on or takes off trousers.

headline: A “white shirt” lost its colour: ワイシャツ is a clipped ホワイトシャツ.

sources.quote: Japanese ワイシャツ
Clipping of ホワイトシャツ (howaito shatsu), borrowed from English white shirt, from the typical white color of dress shirts.
The meaning in Japanese evolved over time to extend first to any dress shirt, regardless of color, and then to any long-sleeved button-down shirt in general.

First cited to 1912. Natsume Sōseki uses the term in his 1915 book 道草 (Michikusa, “Grass on the Wayside”) with the spelling 白襯衣 (literally “white + shirt”), using furigana to indicate a pronunciation of ワイシャツ (waishatsu).

headline: A mansion that shrank into an apartment: the word was meant to sound luxurious.

sources.quote: Borrowed from English mansion. The term gained currency in the latter half of the 1950s, used to lend an air of luxury to high-density residential development projects.
Note that while English mansion most commonly means “large house”, it is also occasionally used to mean “luxurious apartment”, and this latter usage was borrowed into Japanese.

headline: Often called “fake English”, サラリーマン may be real English with a letter dropped.

sources.quote: First cited to 1924 in the novel Chijin no Ai (published in English as Naomi) by Jun’ichirō Tanizaki.

Although often described as wasei eigo (和製英語), this appears to derive from the English phrase salaried man, which appears in print at least as early as 1828. Additionally, the English noun phrase “salary man” also predates the Japanese term. The resulting Japanese term was reimported into English as a compound in the late 20th century.
The form is a regular phonological clipping of the borrowed phrase, dropping the English past‐participle suffix to fit Japanese phonotactics, analyzable as サラリー (sararī) + マン (-man).

The term began to be used in the Taishō period and became firmly established by the early Shōwa period. Prior to its popularization, terms such as 月給取り, 俸給生活者, and 勤め人 were used for similar workers, alongside more derogatory terms like 腰弁当 and 洋服細民. Around 1960, the term ビジネスマン (bijinesuman) also started being used to avoid the mediocre image associated with this word.

headline: めがね was “eye metal” first; the kanji came from Chinese later.

sources.quote: Probably originally a compound of 目 (me, “eye”) + 金 (kane, “metal”, in reference to the metal used in eyeglass frames). The kane changes to gane as an instance of rendaku (連濁). The spelling is based on an apparent borrowing from Chinese, see the gankyō reading below.
Appears in texts from the late 1500s.

headline: The kanji say “soil” and “produce”; the likely origin is a shrine's “small box”.

sources.quote: Probably a compound of 宮 (miya, “shrine”) + 笥 (ke, “small box”).
The ke changes to ge as an instance of rendaku (連濁).

headline: いなか began as “winaka”, and its kanji came from a Chinese word.

sources.quote: /winaka/ → /inaka/
Possibly a compound of 居 (i, the 未然形 (mizenkei, “incomplete form”) and 連用形 (ren'yōkei, “stem form”) of verb 居る (iru), “to be, exist (of animate objects)”) + 中 (naka, “inside, middle”).
The spelling is from Chinese 田舍 (tiánshè).

headline: Brothers have two readings, and they come from two waves of Chinese.

sources.quote: From 兄 (kyō, “elder brother”, goon) + 弟 (dai, “younger brother”, goon), from Middle Chinese 兄弟.

headline: Soy sauce is “thick paste + oil”, and its sound has smoothed from /ɕauju/ to /ɕoːju/.

sources.quote: /ɕauju/ → /ɕɔːju/ → /ɕoːju/
First attested in the mid-Muromachi period.
Orthographic borrowing from Chinese 醬油 /酱油 (literally “thick paste + oil”).

headline: Buckwheat noodles carry a word whose root may be a “corner” — or a “feather”.

sources.quote: Not attested until the middle of the Muromachi period (1336–1573), as a shortening of older 蕎麦 (soba mugi, literally “soba grain”).
Two theories exist regarding the ultimate derivation of the soba element:
* Samuel Martin reconstructs soba as Proto-Japonic *sonpa and derives it as a compound of *so (unknown) + *pa (“feather”). The *pa changes to *ⁿba as an instance of rendaku (連濁).
* From 稜 (soba, “an edge, a corner”), in reference to the seed of the plant being a triangular oval shape with protruding corners.
Considering the late appearance of soba in isolation with the meaning of buckwheat, and the attested earlier senses of side; corner, edge, Martin's reconstruction seems unlikely.
The kanji spelling is an example of jukujikun (熟(じゅく)字(じ)訓(くん)), from 蕎 (“buckwheat”) + 麦 (“wheat”).
